newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook-Copper seeks clues of China moves.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook-Copper seeks clues of China moves.

text.p: Metals markets this week will be watching for any sign of Chinese activity in copper after prices failed an attempt to punch above the $2,400 level.
LME three months copper leapt to $2,445 a tonne on Friday, but the upside break was not sustained and prices tumbled back to the high $2,300s.
Bulls have been expecting the Chinese to enter the market to replenish strategic stockpiles following their New Year celebrations last month.
"However, since their return from holiday, the Chinese have been noted by their absence," said analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff.
This was not surprising, however, since there had been good Chinese buying in the months ahead of the New Year holiday and players might now be awaiting lower prices, he added.
An executive with a European metals producer in Shanghai told Reuters last week that Chinese buyers might be waiting for a pullback to $2,200 to $2,100.

"Conceivably, they may be able to wait until the anticipated new capacity impacts upon the market and postpone their purchases," Squires said, adding that better scrap availability had reduced Chinese reliance on refined metal.
But Japanese buyers might take up any slack as they loaded up ahead of the GSP duty free deadline in April, Merrill Lynch metals analyst Ted Arnold said in his latest research report.

"Our advice to speculators remains unchanged. Do not short copper. More price spikes are possible," said Arnold, who boosted the top end of his expected trading range for the next two months by $200 to $2,500.

But some in Asia were expecting weakness after traders told Reuters in Shanghai last week that Chinese producers could soon start selling to take advantage of high prices. Producer selling had already been seen on the domestic market, they added.
Chartists pegged support around $2,350, followed by $2,313 and $2,300.
Aluminium was appearing tired at higher levels after a disappointing stocks decline of 1,800 tonnes on Friday.
"The big question for the market is whether the recent shift of aluminium out of the LME to the US is ending," broker GNI said in a commentary.
Prices briefly touched a 14-month peak of $1,701 on Tuesday, but quickly got knocked off the higher levels.
Prices needed to break above $1,710 to excite the bulls and resume their upward track.
Aluminium also bounced with copper on Friday, only to fall back. Below the market, support was pegged at $1,634 and $1,612.
